newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-FIVE NATIONS FAREWELL TO STADIUMS.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-FIVE NATIONS FAREWELL TO STADIUMS.

text.p: So much nostalgia is swirling around the final weekend of rugby union's 1997 Five Nations' Championship that events at Parc des Princes and Cardiff Arms Park on Saturday are in danger of being overshadowed by record levels of misty-eyed reminiscence.

England's visit to Wales will be the last international before bulldozers move in to demolish the National Stadium in its current form while France, attempting to land the Grand Slam for the first time since 1987, will bid au revoir to the Parc as an international rugby venue after their encounter with Scotland.

Stadiums can be rebuilt and teams relocated -- in France's case to the new Stade de France built in the northern Parisian suburb of St Denis for the 1998 soccer World Cup -- but this weekend also offers a likely farewell to three of the European game's most recognisable players.

The final whistle will signal the end of the great Jonathan Davies' international career at the age of 34, with former England captain Will Carling acknowledging that it will probably be his Five Nations swansong too.

There is also the unexpected sight of Rob Andrew back in an England squad for what he insists is a "one-off" occasion almost 18 months after his retirement from test rugby. It all prompts an end-of-an-era feel which might even stir a degree of sentimentality in the southern hemisphere.

Nothing in Cardiff on Saturday will surely compare with Gareth Edwards's dive into immortality for the Barbarians against New Zealand in 1973, or even 18-year-old Keith Jarrett's spectacular 19-point haul against England in 1967 which helped add to the Arms Park mystique.

The Parc des Princes faithful will similarly have to rely on their memories of Serge Blanco, Jean-Pierre Rives or Philippe Sella in full cry, although Scotland would enjoy a repeat of their Gavin Hastings-inspired Paris win of two years ago.

That 23-21 victory was Scotland's first on French soil since 1969 but the odds of a repeat and an end of French hopes of a fifth grand slam, following those of 1968, 1977, 1981 and 1987, have narrowed slightly in the past 10 days.

France have been forced to make changes at half-back and in the front-row to the side which came back from 20-6 down to beat England in the last 20 minutes at Twickenham, while Scotland have named the same personnel who downed the Irish by a record 38-10 margin.
Even if France did lose in Paris it is by no means certain that England will score the Cardiff win they would need to steal the title on points difference.
They have called in Leicester's Austin Healey, likened to Australia's David Campese for his speed and confidence in his own ability, for a first start at scrum-half.
And Mike Catt returns at fly-half to replace the injured Paul Grayson, with the 34-year-old Andrew on the bench.
The new-look partnership will find a Welsh side determined to bolster a hitherto mixed season.

Injuries have forced Wales to delay naming their side but there is still scope for one last piece of magic from Davies at fly-half. It is 12 years since he made a try-scoring debut in a red jersey against England in Cardiff and, although he insists he will not play for Wales again, he has still not given up hope of gaining a place on the Lions tour to South Africa.
Neither have a clutch of English and Welsh players, although one of the apparent certainties, Jeremy Guscott, is still glued to the English replacements' bench.
Carling, in contrast, is still in the team but has rejected any chance of travelling with the Lions in favour of a holiday with his girlfriend.

The 31-year-old Carling intends to play on with Harlequins but acknowledges that his 72nd appearance for his country could well be his last. "That is the way I am inclined at the moment but I won't make any definite decision until I have thought long and hard about it during the summer," he said.

So it looks like farewell then to captain Carling and the darting Davies as well as the passion and percussion of the Parc and the Park. It is now up to the new breed of players and architects to fill the gaps.
